title: Welsh Rarebit
subtitle: Grilled cheese sauce on toast with mustard and beer
excerpt: A thick, savoury cheese sauce made with cheddar, mustard, beer, and egg yolk, grilled on thick toast until bubbling and brown-spotted. Faster than it sounds and far better than cheese on toast.
sourceNotes: Eliza Acton, Modern Cookery for Private Families (1845), Project Gutenberg. Welsh rabbit entry: cheese melted with beer and mustard poured over toast. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Toasted cheese and rabbit variants. The distinction between 'Welsh rabbit' and 'Welsh rarebit' is largely a matter of tradition; the two names describe the same dish.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The cheese sauce can be made and kept in the fridge for up to two days. Spread it on toast and grill just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cooked mixture of equal parts butter and flour, used as a thickener for sauces. For Welsh rarebit the roux cooks for only a minute before the liquid goes in, which keeps the sauce light.

content.text: Welsh rarebit is a thick, sharp cheese sauce spooned over toast and grilled until brown and bubbling. The sauce is made with a brief

, melted cheese, a splash of beer, mustard, and Worcestershire sauce. It takes about ten minutes start to finish. This is not the same as cheese on toast: the sauce is thick enough to spread and holds its shape under the grill.
Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add {{plain-flour}} of flour and stir for one minute to cook the roux.
Pour in {{beer}} of beer a little at a time, stirring after each addition. The sauce will be very thick at first; keep stirring until it is smooth and glossy.

Take the pan off the heat. Add {{cheddar}} of grated mature cheddar and stir until fully melted. Stir in {{english-mustard}} of mustard, {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce, and the egg yolk. Season with black pepper. Taste and adjust the mustard if you like a sharper edge.
Heat the grill to high. Toast the bread on both sides until golden. Lay the slices on a grill tray.
Spoon the cheese sauce thickly onto the toast, spreading it right to the edges so it does not burn. Grill for 2 to 3 minutes until the top is brown in patches and starting to bubble.
Eat straight away. Let the rarebit cool even for two minutes and the sauce sets firm.

rows.cause: Cheese added while the pan was still over the heat, causing the fat to separate
rows.fix: Take the pan off the heat before adding the cheese. Stir steadily rather than quickly.

rows.symptom: Sauce is too thick to spread
rows.cause: Too little beer, or the roux cooked for too long
rows.fix: Add another splash of beer and stir over low heat to loosen. The sauce should be thick but spreadable.

rows.cause: Grill not hot enough, or sauce spread too thinly
rows.fix: Preheat the grill for at least 3 minutes before putting the rarebit under it. The sauce needs to be at least 5 mm thick to brown properly.

rows.cause: Toast was too thin or not dry enough before the sauce went on
rows.fix: Use thick-cut bread and toast it fully on both sides before spreading the sauce.

content.text: Buck rarebit: add a poached egg on top of the grilled cheese. Yorkshire rarebit: use stout instead of ale and skip the egg yolk. Lancashire rarebit: stir a pinch of cayenne into the sauce for a sharper heat.

Welsh rarebit appears under the name 'Welsh rabbit' in British cookbooks from the early eighteenth century onwards. The joke name was common: the dish was an affordable substitute for meat at a time when rabbit was itself a poor-man's protein. It has since moved from the supper table to the pub-lunch menu and back again. It is one of the few British dishes that requires no apology.
